newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Brussels Eurocrats to move back to old HQ in 2000.
newsitem.headline: Brussels Eurocrats to move back to old HQ in 2000.

text.p: The European Commission said on Monday it had agreed to move back into and buy the landmark Berlaymont building in Brussels which 3,000 eurocrats were forced to leave in 1992 because of an asbestos scare.

Erkki Liikanen, Commissioner responsible for budgetary and administrative affairs, told a news conference the move would take place in summer 2000 once work to remove the asbestos and refurbish the building had been completed.

Liikanen said the total cost of renovating the 30-year-old, 128,000 square metre building would be 375 million Ecus ($420 million), a bill which has at present been met mostly by the Belgian state and the building's private shareholders, banks Bacob and ASLK-CGER.
Liikanen said the Commission would pay back the sum over 27 years after which it would own the building.

"The Commission's policy on property is to become owner of a significant part of its office space in the long run. This will generate savings and enable us to take more responsibility for urban development," Liikanen said.
The final signature of the definitive long lease agreement, between the Belgian state and Commission is programmed for 2000.

"The refurbished Berlaymont will give the Commission's presence in Brussels a tangible image," Belgian Public Affairs Minister Andre Flahaut said. "It will be a landmark and embody present-day aspirations together with the preservation of the environment".

Among the main features of the new building would be its colour. Exterior blinds designed to shield staff from sunlight would make it appear white, in contrast to the infamous black-glass exterior of the original.

"The facade will look pure and white, not unlike the effect created by the current "white" wrapping," the Commission said, referring to the shroud that has covered the building since work to remove asbestos started in 1994.

The conversion would leave the building, which takes its name from a convent demolished to make way for its erection, "green" and functional, in line with the ethos for the third millenium," the Commission added.
As well as housing some 2,750 civil servants, the building would boast the world's largest press centre.
The Commission decided to leave the Berlaymont in May 1991 after receiving an unpublished report into the health threat posed to its staff by the presence of the asbestos.
